extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters (esp. New York) engaged in the 1787–1788 constitutional debate / general readership interested in design of national government
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate structural defects of a confederate national government (the Articles of Confederation) and the essential powers and institutional arrangements required for a functional Union. The piece argues which powers are necessary and why existing arrangements fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction to its laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States, as now composed, have no powers to exact obedience, or punish disobedience to their resolutions, either by pecuniary mulcts, by a suspension or divestiture of privileges, or by any other constitutional mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the dilemma that without an express delegation to enforce laws the Confederacy is a government 'destitute even of the shadow of constitutional power to enforce the execution of its own laws.' Discusses that implying coercive authority by inference contradicts the clause that each State retains all powers not 'expressly delegated.' Consequences: inability to enforce national resolutions, unique and dangerous anomaly among governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual guaranty of the State governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another capital imperfection in the federal plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues a mutual guaranty is necessary to repel domestic dangers (e.g., usurpation, faction) and to prevent the erection of tyranny within states; such guaranty would operate only against violent changes and would not impede lawful, peaceful reforms. Uses Massachusetts' recent convulsions as an example of the need for such assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for the national government to raise its own revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of steering clear of this inconvenience, but by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends imposts, excises, and duties upon articles of consumption as the primary long-term revenue sources. Explains that these taxes act like a 'fluid' finding its level with means of paying them, and that they self-limit (high duties reduce consumption and thus revenue). Contrasts national taxation with unreliable quotas and requisitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of quotas / requisitions as a fiscal method
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of regulating the contributions of the States to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains there is no common standard to measure national wealth (land value or population are inadequate), so quotas produce glaring inequality and oppression. Quotas have been tried and failed; they risk destruction of the Union when burdens are unfairly distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for indirect taxes (consumption duties) as a secure revenue source
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a signal advantage of taxes on articles of consumption, that they contain in their own nature a security against excess. They prescribe their own limit; which cannot be exceeded without defeating the end proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the economic mechanism: excessive duties reduce consumption and revenue, so indirect taxes naturally limit themselves and are less likely to be oppressive. Argues indirect taxes will long constitute the chief part of national revenue in America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment rule for direct taxes (use of numbers/population)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those of the direct kind, which principally relate to land and buildings, may admit of a rule of apportionment. ... numbers, in the view of simplicity and certainty, are entitled to a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes valuation of land is difficult and costly, especially in a developing country; population (numbers) is simpler and more certain as a rule for apportioning direct taxes when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate commerce (national superintendence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a power to regulate commerce is by all parties allowed to be of the number. ... there is no object, either as it respects the interests of trade or finance, that more strongly demands a federal superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that absence of federal commerce power has prevented beneficial treaties, produced interstate conflicts and dissimilar regulations, and left the Union vulnerable in foreign commercial dealings. Offers examples (state prohibitions, the German empire's multiplicity of duties) and notes foreign nations will be reluctant to form reliable treaties with an inconsistent union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to raise and manage armies (not mere requisitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of raising armies ... is merely a power of making requisitions upon the States for quotas of men. This practice ... was found replete with obstructions to a vigorous and to an economical system of defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details the practical problems caused by requisitions: competition between states producing high bounties, short enlistments, slow levies, fluctuations harming discipline, and unequal burdens depending on proximity to danger. Argues national authority over troops avoids these inefficiencies and inequities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject system of quotas for men or money (inequality and imbecility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of quotas and requisitions, whether it be applied to men or money, is, in every view, a system of imbecility in the Union, and of inequality and injustice among the members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains quotas create injustice (some states overburdened, others underburdened), logistical impossibility of equal levies, and political instability because suffering states may withdraw consent; stresses need for national fiscal and military capacities instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation: oppose equal suffrage among unequal States
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of equal suffrage among the States is another exceptionable part of the Confederation. Every idea of proportion and every rule of fair representation conspire to condemn a principle, which gives to Rhode Island an equal weight ... with Massachusetts ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues equal votes for vastly unequal states contradict principles of republican government (majority rule and fairness). Warns that larger states will revolt at receiving commands from much smaller ones; equal suffrage can result in a minority of people controlling the whole by artificial distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unanimity or excessively high decision thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of unanimity in public bodies, or of something approaching towards it, has been founded upon a supposition that it would contribute to security. But its real operation is to embarrass the administration, to destroy the energy of the government ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains unanimity (or high thresholds) enable obstruction by small minorities, foreign corruption, and delay—examples include the Polish diet analogy and scenarios where allies or foreign powers can more easily corrupt few votes. Argues that requiring a simple majority for many actions increases government effectiveness and security against corruption and paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a judiciary power / supreme tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: A circumstance which crowns the defects of the Confederation remains yet to be mentioned, the want of a judiciary power. Laws are a dead letter without courts to expound and define their true meaning and operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues treaties must be part of the law and their import as to individuals determined by courts. Without a single supreme tribunal, there will be as many different final determinations as there are states, producing confusion, contradictions, bias from local prejudices, and jeopardizing uniformity and foreign confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against foreign corruption and domestic faction
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the weak sides of republics ... is that they afford too easy an inlet to foreign corruption. ... deputies of the United Provinces have, in various instances, been purchased by the emissaries of the neighboring kingdoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical examples (United Provinces, Sweden) to show vulnerability of republican representatives to bribery. Advocates institutional designs (majority decision rules, stable national structures) that reduce the ease with which small numbers can be corrupted to frustrate national interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate organization of Congress to exercise national powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The organization of Congress is itself utterly improper for the exercise of those powers which are necessary to be deposited in the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the essay breaks off before full exposition, it asserts that the structural organization (composition, voting rules, procedures) of the national legislature must be suited to enable it to exercise the powers required by the Union — otherwise powers delegated are ineffectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting violence for law; prefer magistracy-based coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities ... is subversive of the order and ends of civil polity, by substituting VIOLENCE in place of LAW, or the destructive COERCION of the SWORD in place of the mild and salutary COERCION of the MAGISTRACY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that a federal authority that operates as a sovereign over sovereign states risks relying on force rather than legal magistracy; the implication is to design institutions that secure compliance via lawful magistracy and constitutional mechanisms, limiting the need for direct coercive force.
